message.content:
**The three major schisms that have shaped Christian history** | # | Schism | Approximate Date | Key Causes & Consequences | |---|--------|------------------|---------------------------| | 1 | **Great Schism (East–West Schism)** | 1054 CE | • Long‑standing theological, liturgical, and political differences between the Byzantine (Eastern) and Latin (Western) churches.
• Disputes over papal primacy, the Filioque clause, and ecclesiastical jurisdiction.
• Resulted in the formal split into the Roman Catholic Church (West) and the Eastern Orthodox Church (East). | | 2 | **Protestant Reformation** | 1517–1648 CE | • Initiated by Martin Luther’s 95 Theses (1517) and spread through calls for reform in doctrine, practice, and church governance.
• Key issues: indulgences, authority of Scripture vs. tradition, justification by faith, and the role of the clergy.
• Led to the creation of numerous Protestant denominations (Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican, Anabaptist, etc.) and significant religious, political, and cultural upheaval across Europe. | | 3 | **East–West Schism of 1965 (Ecumenical Movement & Modern Schisms)** | 1965 CE (and ongoing) | • While not a single “schism” like the previous two, the 20th‑century ecumenical movement highlighted deep divisions within Christianity, especially between the Roman Catholic Church and various Protestant and Orthodox groups.
• The 1965 *Decree on Ecumenical Relations* (Papal decree) and subsequent dialogues (e.g., *Unitatis Redintegratio*, *Nostra Aetate*) sought to heal divisions but also exposed persistent theological differences.
• Modern schisms include the split of the Old Catholic Church, the formation of independent evangelical churches, and the ongoing separation between the Oriental Orthodox and Eastern Orthodox churches. | These three events—each involving profound theological, liturgical, and institutional disagreements—are widely regarded as the most consequential schisms in Christian history.
